To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) parents who have more wealth and are in better health are more likely to leave a bequest; (2) parents who are more educated and have more children are more likely to make a bequest, and the number of children has a stronger effect for women than for men; (3) children’s education and wealth are not significantly related to the probability of receiving a bequest; and (4) children’s health is positively related to the probability that they receive a bequest, especially

parents who have more children and more grandchildren are more likely to bequeath, and that parents are less likely to leave a bequest when they are in poor health and when they have more children and grandchildren.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether parents are more likely to bequeath to children who are more likely to do good things for them.
the question of how parents decide who should inherit their property, and why.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
parents are not purely altruistic, and do not simply use bequests to reward children for good behavior.

the results of the study are consistent with the predictions of the theory of altruistic behavior, and are consistent with the prediction of the strategic bequest motive theory that the size of the bequest is inversely related to the child's provision of care to the parent.
the data do not support the theory of altruistic parents who give equal bequests to children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results are mixed, with some evidence supporting each of the theories. 2 2.
the results are mixed and that the data are not rich enough to distinguish clearly between theories.
the data are consistent with the idea that bequest motives are complex, and that parents use their wealth strategically to induce children and other family members to provide care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Mexican Health and Ageing Study (MHAS) is an excellent resource for the study of bequests.
parents are strategic when making their bequest decisions, and this is consistent with the theory developed by Bernheim et al..
